comment: The single declaration of every dependency a conver project has. Adding a dependency means adding one entry here — never a new mechanism. `requiredFor` says which rotation needs it; `providedBy` names the ticket that introduces it, so an entry whose ticket has not converged is reported as not yet required rather than as missing. The three sections differ in what resolving an entry means: `npmRoots` are trees this repository installs and resolves, `tools` are executables it probes, and `propertyEngines` are libraries a generated property is written for, which the subject's own package manager resolves — so this repository records them and probes none of them.

npmRoots.description: The installed .claude tree: ajv for schema validation, sql.js for the state store.
The conver tool itself: the ACP client libraries and node-cron.
Declares ajv. Resolves today only by upward traversal into .claude/node_modules, which is why the root is named explicitly rather than left to where Node happens to look.

The analysis tree: web-tree-sitter as the common syntax layer and the pinned grammar for each of the six target languages. Versions are pinned because a grammar change changes the AST and therefore every measurement taken from it.

The installed `tree-sitter-rust` grammar the reverse rotation parses rust with. Its own manifest declares no dependencies: the packages it is installed beside are declared by the root above, and this entry exists so that a grammar the capability matrix carries is a declared dependency rather than one that happened to be on the machine.

tools.description: Node 22 or later, so that node --test is available.
The layer-C semantic adapter for Rust. Not used by R0-R2.5, which is syntax only; P22-5 is the first consumer. Recorded so the capability is declared rather than assumed.
Go analysis for the six-language toolchain.
Python analysis for the six-language toolchain.
C/C++ analysis for the six-language toolchain.

An optional layer-C capability. Rust support is GA (October 2025, build-free), with measured limits on macro-heavy code, async/await and guarded unsafe. It is not the foundation: see docs/P22-ANALYSIS-TECH.md.
An auxiliary candidate-discovery backend for the languages it covers. Its official frontend has no Rust, so it is not the six-language semantic layer: see docs/P22-ANALYSIS-TECH.md.

propertyEngines.description: The engine R6.5 writes a Rust property for. It is a crate rather than an executable — `PROPERTY_ENGINES` names it, the property E14 writes declares it, and `cargo test` resolves and runs it inside the disposable worktree — so there is no command that reports its version and this entry is recorded rather than probed.

The engine R6.5 writes a TypeScript and a JavaScript property for, resolved by `npm` inside the disposable worktree. It serves two languages and E14 renders it once per language, because a single rendering would write one language's file into the other's tree.

The engine R6.5 writes a Go property for, resolved by `go test` inside the disposable worktree. It is a module rather than an executable, and it declares no version command, so the entry is recorded rather than probed.

The engine R6.5 writes a Python property for, resolved by the interpreter inside the disposable worktree. Hypothesis infers its strategy from a type hint, which is why a parameter carrying none is reported as inexpressible rather than approximated.

The engine R6.5 writes a C/C++ property for, compiled into the disposable worktree by the same CMake project that builds the subject. Its C/C++ results carry the preprocessor boundary until P24-6 resolves which translation units a build actually composes.
